newsitem.title: JAPAN: N.Korea-related Japan bank fails in blow to North.
newsitem.headline: N.Korea-related Japan bank fails in blow to North.

text.p: North Korea suffered an indirect economic blow on Wednesday when a credit union that handles deposits from ethnic Koreans in Japan with families in the impoverished communist nation went bust.
Authorities in Osaka said five North Korea-related credit unions in Japan would merge into a single institution and take over the operations of the troubled Chogin Osaka Shinyo Kumiai.

Unrecoverable loans at Chogin Osaka, which like the other five credit unions is run by North Korean residents in Japan, are estimated at 200 billion yen ($1.69 billion) based on the Osaka prefectural government's financial assessment, officials told a news conference.

Although there is no direct link between the failed credit union and North Korea, pro-North ethnic Koreans are believed to be the largest source of hard currency for the Stalinist state, which is on the brink of famine after two years of devastating floods and a longer period of economic decline.

The credit union failure, blamed mainly on problem loans that ballooned after Japan's asset bubble burst in 1990, follows other financial blows for North Korea, whose economy shrank for the seventh year running in 1996, according to South Korean official estimates.

North Korean supporters, who account for about one-third of Japan's 666,000-member ethnic Korean community, are believed to support the North through the General Association of Korean Residents in Japan, Pyongyang's de facto embassy in Japan.

Signs emerged last year, however, that one key source of North Korean funding -- from the "pachinko" slot machine business -- was drying up as mainstream Japanese firms muscled in on what was once a preserve of the ethnic minorities.

The North Korean community's pachinko interests -- a legacy of the early post-war years when Japanese shunned an industry thought of as dirty and cheap -- generate a subsidy to Pyongyang of about $550 million a year, Japan's Public Security Investigation Agency has estimated.
The pachinko fund constitutes a significant portion of the $1.8-$2 billion Japanese and Western intelligence officials estimate Korean residents in Japan remit to Pyongyang annually.

Other sources of cash for North Korea from Japan's ethnic Koreans include two-way trade -- mostly in cheap textiles and foodstuffs, which totalled $600 million in 1995 -- and money carried by the roughly 5,000 Korean residents in Japan who travel to North Korea by ferry each year.
The subsidies by pro-North Koreans in Japan is probably the largest single foreign exchange earner for North Korea, which has been seeking large-scale food aid from the international community.

Last month a North Korean vessel was caught smuggling illegal narcotics into Japan, in what authorities said was a clumsy operation that may have indicated how desperate the defiantly proud country had become.

Last year a North Korean military pharmacist who defected to the South said the country was helping to finance its ruling Workers' Party by exporting opium grown in 10 places in North Korea and processed in a factory northeast of Pyongyang.
